definition: A hypothetical artificial general intelligence that can apply its own intelligence to improving its design, so each round of self-improvement yields a more capable successor.
details: In 1965, Good argued that an “ultraintelligent machine” able to surpass human intellect could design still better machines, triggering a self-amplifying loop often called the intelligence explosion. Recursive general intelligence names that loop explicitly: general problem-solving ability plus the capacity to modify the very system doing the solving. The idea underpins debates about superintelligence and how quickly capabilities might compound.

explainer.lead: A hypothetical general AI that can improve its own design, so each round of self-improvement yields a more capable successor. It matters because it frames debates about how fast capabilities could compound toward superintelligence.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a student who is so good at studying that every time they learn something, they also get better at learning — so their progress keeps speeding up on its own.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers treat it as a thought experiment rather than a buildable system; the pitfall is assuming an intelligence explosion is inevitable, when no such loop has been demonstrated.
tiers.paperLevel: Defined as general problem-solving ability plus the capacity to modify the very system doing the solving; the term names the self-amplifying loop Good described in 1965 as an intelligence explosion. It remains hypothetical, with no observed instance.

explainer.example: Good's 1965 argument: an ultraintelligent machine able to surpass human intellect could design still better machines, triggering a self-amplifying loop.
